'''Albert Roach Hibbs''' (October 19, 1924 &ndash; February 24, 2003) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[physicist]] affiliated with the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] (JPL).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Al Hibbs (1924-2003) {{!}} Scientist, "The Voice of JPL" |url=https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/people/860/al-hibbs-1924-2003/ |access-date=2022-04-05 |website=NASA Solar System Exploration}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Oliver |first=Myrna |date=2003-02-27 |title=Albert Hibbs, 78; JPL Scientist, Voice of Unmanned Missions |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-feb-27-me-hibbs27-story.html |access-date=2022-04-05 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref> He was known as "The Voice of JPL" due to his gift for explaining advanced science in simple terms.<ref name=NASA/> He helped establish JPL's Space Science Division in 1960 and later served as its first chief. He was the systems designer for [[Explorer 1]], the USA's first [[satellite]], and helped establish the framework for exploration of the [[Solar System]] through the 1960s.  Hibbs qualified as an [[astronaut]] in 1967 and was slated to be a crew member of Apollo 25, but he ultimately did not go to the Moon due to the [[Apollo program]] ending after the [[Apollo 17]] mission in 1972.

==Education==

Hibbs earned bachelor's degree in physics from the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech) in 1945, having attended Caltech under the sponsorship of the [[United States Navy|US Navy]]'s [[V-12 Navy College Training Program|V-12 program]].  He then obtained a master's degree in mathematics from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1947.<ref name=NASA>{{cite web |title=Al Hibbs (1924-2003) Scientist, "The Voice of JPL" |url=https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/people/860/al-hibbs-1924-2003/ |website=NASA Science |publisher=Planetary Science Communications team at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory for NASA’s Science Mission Directorate |accessdate=16 December 2019}}</ref><ref name=PhysicsToday/>

While working as a staff member at JPL, in 1955 Hibbs received a PhD in physics from Caltech with a thesis on "The Growth of [[Wind wave|Water Waves Due to the Action of the Wind]]".<ref>{{cite web |title=Albert Roach Hibbs |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=136442 |website=Mathematics Genealogy Project |publisher=Department of Mathematics, North Dakota State University |accessdate=3 June 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Hibbs |first1=Albert |title=The growth of water waves due to the action of the wind |url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/5005/ |website=Caltech THESIS |year=1955 |publisher=California Institute of Technology |doi=10.7907/VT31-VT32 |accessdate=3 June 2020|type=phd }}</ref> His thesis advisor was the Nobel laureate [[Richard Feynman]]. Hibbs became close friends with Feynman and together they published the textbook ''Quantum Mechanics and Path Integrals'' (McGraw-Hill, 1965),<ref name=OAC>{{cite web |title=Albert R. Hibbs Papers: Finding Aid |url=https://oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/c8c8280r/entire_text/ |website=Online Archive of California |publisher=The Huntington Library, San Marino, California |accessdate=7 February 2020}}</ref><ref name=PhysicsToday/> which is still a standard reference on the [[path integral formulation]].

==Career==
Hibbs joined the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in 1950. He became head of JPL's Research and Analysis Section, and in this role, he was the systems designer for America's first successful satellite, [[Explorer 1]], in 1958. After [[NASA]] took over JPL in 1958, Hibbs worked to establish the framework for planetary missions for the next decade.<ref name=PhysicsToday>{{cite journal |last1=Pickering |first1=William H |title=Albert Roach Hibbs |journal=Physics Today |year=2004 |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=68–69 |publisher=American Institute of Physics |doi=10.1063/1.1650081 |bibcode=2004PhT....57a..68P }}</ref>

In 1960, Hibbs was placed in charge of forming and leading the Space Science Division at JPL. As the division became successful, Hibbs emerged as the "Voice of JPL".<ref name=OAC/>

From 1962 to 1967, Hibbs left JPL to work on special assignment as staff scientist for the Arms Control Study Group (ACSG) of the U.S. [[Arms Control and Disarmament Agency]] (ACDA), studying how arms-control treaties could be monitored from space.<ref name=snac>{{cite web |title=Hibbs, Albert R., 1924-2003 |url=https://snaccooperative.org/ark:/99166/w6578z1v |website=snac |publisher=Social Networks and Archival Context |accessdate=3 June 2020}}</ref>

From the late 1960s to the 1980s, he became the authoritative source of information on JPL missions, including: the [[Ranger program|Ranger]] and [[Surveyor program|Surveyor]] missions to the [[Moon]]; the [[Mariner program|Mariner]] missions to [[Venus]], [[Mars]], and [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]]; the [[Viking program|Viking]] missions to Mars; and the [[Voyager program|Voyager]] missions to the outer planets.<ref name=PhysicsToday/><ref name=caltech_obituary/>

By the age of five, Hibbs had decided that he wanted to go to the Moon.<ref name=caltech_obituary/> He qualified as an astronaut in 1967, despite being 7 years over the age limit, and he was slated to be a crew member of [[Canceled Apollo missions|Apollo 25]]. The [[Apollo program]] ended after [[Apollo 17]], denying him his dream.<ref name=caltech_obituary/> Nevertheless, he has reflected that: "Even though I didn't make it to the moon, my machines did."<ref>{{cite web |title=Science Quotes by Albert Hibbs |url=https://todayinsci.com/H/Hibbs_Albert/HibbsAlbert-Quotations.htm |website=Today in Science History |publisher=Todayinsci |accessdate=3 June 2020}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Hibbs hosted and produced several radio and television programs for adults and children. He won a [[Peabody Awards|Peabody award]] for the children's series ''[[Exploring (TV series)|Exploring]]'', as well as two Thomas Alva Edison Foundation National Media Awards. He was also given NASA's Exceptional Service Medal, "for his outstanding achievements in explaining the complexities and significance of space exploration to the general public via radio and television," and the NASA Achievement Award.<ref name=caltech_obituary>{{cite web|url=http://eands.caltech.edu/articles/LXVI/alhibbs.html|title=Al Hibbs (1924–2003):obituary|publisher=Caltech|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100624185840/http://eands.caltech.edu/articles/LXVI/alhibbs.html|archivedate=June 24, 2010 
}}</ref><ref name=NASAVideo>{{cite web |title=In Memoriam: Al Hibbs |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/video/details.php?id=196 |website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory |publisher=Jet Propulsion Laboratory |accessdate=3 June 2020}}</ref><ref name=snac/>

As a prominent member of the [[The Skeptics Society|Southern California Skeptics]], Hibbs was awarded a Fellowship from the [[Committee for Skeptical Inquiry|Committee for the Scientific Investigation of Claims of the Paranormal (CSICOP)]].<ref name=snac/>

Hibbs also had an asteroid named after him (2441 Hibbs) in honor of Al Hibbs and his wife Marka as an acknowledgement of the role they played in introducing her to Space Science at Caltech.<ref>{{Citation|chapter=(2441) Hibbs|date=2007|title=Dictionary of Minor Planet Names|pages=199|editor-last=Schmadel|editor-first=Lutz D.|publisher=Springer|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-29925-7_2442|isbn=978-3-540-29925-7|doi-access=free}}</ref>{{Clarify|reason=Unclear role of wife here, generally unclear sentence|date=April 2022}}

==Other activities==
In 1947, Hibbs and [[Roy Walford]] took time off from graduate and medical school, respectively, to go to [[Reno, Nevada|Reno]] and [[Las Vegas, Nevada|Las Vegas]] to beat the [[casino]]s at [[roulette]]. Studying biases in the roulette wheels, they made profits variously estimated between $6,500<ref name=Life1947>{{cite magazine|title=How to Win $6,500 - Two student theoreticians invent system for beating roulette wheel |magazine=[[Life (magazine)|Life Magazine]] |date=December 8, 1947 |page=46 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nlIEAAAAMBAJ&q=walford&pg=PA46 | accessdate=May 18, 2016 }}</ref> and $42,000.<ref name=LATimes2004>{{cite news | title=Roy Walford, 79; Eccentric UCLA Scientist Touted Food Restriction | date=May 1, 2004 | author=Maugh, Thomas H. II |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-may-01-me-walford1-story.html |access-date=May 18, 2016}}</ref> According to Hibbs himself, during an episode of ''[[You Bet Your Life]]'' on which he was a contestant and won $250, he made "about $12,000" from his roulette exploits.<ref>{{cite AV media |url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcxxzJLzVBs | title = You Bet Your Life #58-18 | date=January 22, 1959 |time=3:08}}</ref> The pair used the profits to spend over a year sailing around the Caribbean aboard a 40-foot sailboat, Adonde.<ref name=OAC/>

While working for JPL, Hibbs appeared on ''[[You Bet Your Life]]'' where he talked about his adventures in roulette.<ref>"[https://www.forbes.com/sites/startswithabang/2017/05/23/how-physicists-used-science-to-beat-the-odds-at-roulette/?sh=51afae7a3c39 Isaac Newton Vs. Las Vegas: How Physicists Used Science To Beat The Odds At Roulette]" by Paul Halpern, ''Forbes'', 23 May 2017. Accessed December 29, 2023. ([https://tubitv.com/tv-shows/277361/s01-e18-season-1-episode-18 The episode], as available on Tubi.)</ref>

Hibbs was a member of the project review committee for [[Biosphere 2]] from 1987 to 1992 and was involved in artist [[Tom Van Sant]]'s [https://vimeo.com/50738196 Geosphere Project] from 1989 to 1995 as a member of the Eyes on Earth Board of Directors.<ref name=OAC/> In his retirement, Hibbs pursued underwater photography at sites all over the world.<ref name=PhysicsToday/>

Hibbs enjoyed making [[kinetic sculpture]] as a hobby<ref name="snac" /> and was fascinated by miniaturised, independently operating machines—a field where he once again collaborated in a well known idea-experiment of Feynman's. According to Feynman, it was Hibbs who originally suggested to him (circa 1959) the idea of a medical use for Feynman's theoretical micromachines (see [[nanotechnology]]). Hibbs suggested that certain repair machines might one day be reduced in size to the point that it would, in theory, be possible to (as Feynman put it) "swallow the doctor".<ref>{{cite web
 |url         = http://www.its.caltech.edu/~feynman/plenty.html
 |title       = Plenty of Room at the Bottom
 |author      = Richard P. Feynman
 |date        = December 1959
 |accessdate  = March 18, 2010
 |archiveurl  = https://web.archive.org/web/20100211190050/http://www.its.caltech.edu/~feynman/plenty.html
 |archivedate = February 11, 2010
 |url-status     = dead
 |df          = mdy-all
}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Hibbs first married in 1950, to Florence Pavin, with whom he had two children. He was widowed in 1970. In 1971, he married Marka Oliver.

He died in February 2003 from complications following heart surgery at Huntington Memorial Hospital in Pasadena, California.<ref name="OAC" />
